Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Luke 3, drawing on the sources I was able to access.

---

## Luke 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### vv. 1–2a: The Historical Setting

Luke anchors John's ministry in secular history by naming seven rulers — one emperor (Tiberius), one governor (Pilate), three tetrarchs (Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias), and two high priests (Annas and Caiaphas). This is the mark of a careful historian and signals that the gospel enters real, datable history, not myth. All these rulers were known for cruelty, corruption, or moral degradation. Tiberius was a severe emperor; Pilate was notorious for brutal massacres of Jews; the Herodian family was steeped in corruption. The gospel arrived in a world that desperately needed it. The "fifteenth year of Tiberius" yields a date somewhere between AD 26 and 29 depending on whether one reckons from his co-regency with Augustus (AD 11/12) or his sole reign after Augustus's death (AD 14).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-3-commentary

Luke mentions both Annas and Caiaphas as high priest. Although Caiaphas was officially the high priest (AD 18–36), Annas his father-in-law had been deposed by the Romans in AD 15 but remained the real power behind the priesthood. This dual reference highlights the corruption and power-politics within the Jewish religious leadership.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-3-commentary

---

### vv. 2b–3: John's Call and Message

**"The word of God came to John"** — This phrase echoes the call of Old Testament prophets (e.g., Jeremiah 1:2, Hosea 1:1). Luke uses the Greek word *rhema* (spoken word), and this description of how John's ministry began is unique to Luke's Gospel. John had lived in the wilderness since his youth (Luke 1:80), and now God's prompting word launched his public work.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-3-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

**"A baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins"** — John's baptism was shocking for Jews, because baptism (ceremonial immersion) was a rite for Gentile converts to Judaism. For a Jew to submit to it was to say, "I am as spiritually unclean as a pagan and need cleansing." Repentance (*metanoia*) is primarily a change of mind and direction — not merely feeling sorry but turning around. The word "forgiveness" (*aphesis*) carries the idea of release, remission, or liberty — sin being sent away like the scapegoat (Leviticus 16).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-3-commentary

John Piper (Reformed Baptist) emphasises that repentance here means "turning away from any and all reliance upon what I am by birth or what I have done by my own effort, and turning to the absolutely free mercy of God for the hope of salvation."

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/john-the-baptist-and-the-brood-of-vipers

---

### vv. 4–6: The Isaiah Prophecy

Luke alone among the Gospel writers extends the Isaiah 40 quotation to include verses 4–5 ("Every valley shall be filled … all flesh shall see the salvation of God"). Matthew and Mark quote only Isaiah 40:3. Luke's longer citation makes the point that the Messiah's coming brings salvation available to **all humanity** ("all flesh"), not just to Israel. This is a key theme of Luke's Gospel: the universality of the gospel.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-3-commentary
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/john-the-baptist-and-the-brood-of-vipers

The imagery of filling valleys, levelling mountains, and straightening crooked roads signifies that the coming of the Messiah involves radical transformation — removing every obstacle between humanity and God. John's message was that the real problem was not "them" (the Romans) but "me" — each person must get right with God.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### v. 7: "You Brood of Vipers!"

John calls the crowds a "brood of vipers" — a stunningly blunt opening. In Genesis 3, the serpent (viper) is identified with Satan, and God speaks of enmity between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed. Calling the crowds "brood of vipers" is equivalent to calling them children of the devil (cf. John 8:44, where Jesus says the same). John's first word is an indictment: "You are people in Satan's grip."

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/john-the-baptist-and-the-brood-of-vipers

**"Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?"** — John questions the crowds' motives. Wrath is real and coming. Yet the fact that they are coming for baptism suggests they are fleeing in the right direction — toward repentance and forgiveness.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/john-the-baptist-and-the-brood-of-vipers
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### v. 8: "Bear Fruits Worthy of Repentance"

Genuine repentance always produces visible fruit. The call to "produce fruit" is a call to demonstrate the reality of inward change through outward actions. John then attacks the deeply held Jewish belief that descent from Abraham guaranteed salvation. Some rabbinic teaching held that Abraham's merits were sufficient for any Jew's salvation and that no descendant of Abraham could go to hell.

John Piper explains: "God can raise up from these stones sons of Abraham" means God's mercy is so free and powerful that He can make anybody — Jew or Gentile — a true child of Abraham. Jewishness is no guarantee, and non-Jewishness is no hindrance.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-the-fruit-that-befits-repentance
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### v. 9: The Axe at the Root

The image of the axe already laid at the root means judgment is imminent, not distant. Every tree not producing good fruit faces destruction. The "fire" here is judgment — not purifying but destructive fire. This is the fire of hell for those who do not repent.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### vv. 10–11: The Crowd's Question — Sharing

When the crowd asks "What then should we do?", John's answer is notably ordinary: share clothing and food. Repentance is demonstrated not in dramatic gestures but in everyday integrity and generosity. Having two tunics (an inner garment) when someone has none is a concrete test. John Piper notes that all three of John's sample exhortations (to the crowd, tax collectors, and soldiers) concern money and possessions — because "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Luke 12:34).

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-the-fruit-that-befits-repentance
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### vv. 12–13: Tax Collectors — Honesty

Tax collectors (publicans) were Jews who collected taxes for the Roman occupiers. Because the Romans auctioned tax-collection rights to the highest bidder, collectors made their profit by extracting more than was due — and were intensely hated as greedy collaborators. John does not tell them to leave their profession but to stop exploiting it: "Collect no more than you are authorized." Integrity in a despised profession is fruit of repentance.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-the-fruit-that-befits-repentance

---

### v. 14: Soldiers — Contentment and Fairness

The soldiers who came were likely not Roman legionaries but auxiliary troops (possibly Jewish or Gentile) serving under Herod Antipas or in local policing roles. John gives three commands: (1) do not extort money by violence or intimidation, (2) do not accuse falsely (likely to obtain bribes), and (3) be content with your wages. Piper notes that this last command echoes Hebrews 13:5 — discontent with wages reveals a heart not resting in God's provision.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-the-fruit-that-befits-repentance
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### vv. 15–16: Is John the Christ? — John's Humility

The people were "waiting expectantly" and wondering if John himself might be the Messiah. John immediately deflects: he baptises with mere water, but the Coming One is "more powerful" — so great that John is unworthy even to untie His sandal strap. In rabbinic culture, a disciple could be required to do almost anything for his teacher *except* remove his sandals — that was considered too degrading. John's self-assessment is therefore radical humility.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

**"He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire."**

This is one of the most debated verses across traditions:

**Pentecostal / Charismatic view (Assemblies of God):** The "baptism in the Holy Spirit" is a distinct, post-conversion experience, evidenced initially by speaking in tongues, empowering believers for witness and charismatic ministry. It is the fulfilment of Joel 2:28–29. Fire represents the Spirit's purifying and empowering presence, as seen at Pentecost when "tongues of fire" appeared (Acts 2:3).

- https://ag.org/en/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Baptism-in-the-Holy-Spirit

**Reformed view (Ligonier):** The baptism of the Holy Spirit is not a post-conversion second blessing but is the once-for-all work of Christ in uniting believers to His body at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13). The "fire" refers to judgment for those who reject the gospel — the same Messiah who baptises some with the Spirit will baptise others with the fire of judgment. Fire in the immediate context (v. 17) is the unquenchable fire that consumes the chaff.

- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/baptism-of-the-holy-spirit
- https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ask-ligonier/what-did-john-the-baptist-mean-when-he-said-jesus-would-baptize-with-fire

**Classic interpretation (Pulpit Commentary, older sources):** The fire is not punitive but purifying — the flame of purification that Messiah brings alongside the Spirit. This view sees "fire" as refining fire that burns away sin in the believer, not the fire of judgment. The Pulpit Commentary explicitly rejects the punitive interpretation as "quite alien from the context."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/3.htm

**Holman Bible Dictionary:** Being baptised with the Holy Spirit and fire means being immersed in the presence of God so that one becomes aware of sin and the need for cleansing. Fire in Israel's worship represented both God's presence, judgment on sin, and purification of the repentant.

- https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hbd/b/baptism-of-fire.html

---

### v. 17: Winnowing Fork — Separation and Judgment

The Messiah holds a winnowing fork to separate wheat from chaff. The wheat (the repentant, the true children of Abraham by faith) is gathered into the barn. The chaff (the unrepentant) is burned with "unquenchable fire" — a clear image of final judgment and hell. This verse strongly supports the interpretation that the "fire" of v. 16 includes judgment.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-the-fruit-that-befits-repentance

---

### v. 18: "He Preached Good News"

Luke calls John's message — despite its warnings of wrath, vipers, axes, and unquenchable fire — "good news" (*euangelion*). John Piper notes three reasons: (1) a warning about coming wrath is good news when escape is offered; (2) it is good news that the way to forgiveness is simply to rest in God's free mercy, open to all; (3) exhortations to live a certain way are good news because they help us test the genuineness of our faith and guide us into the way of deepest joy.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/what-is-the-fruit-that-befits-repentance

---

### vv. 19–20: John's Imprisonment

John publicly rebuked Herod Antipas for taking his brother Philip's wife Herodias. Under Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21, a man taking his brother's wife was specifically forbidden while the brother lived. This was a bold, costly stand for truth. Luke places John's imprisonment here, **before** narrating Jesus' baptism (v. 21), even though chronologically John's imprisonment occurred later. John Piper argues Luke does this to emphasise the sharp break between John's era (the law and prophets) and Jesus' era (the kingdom of God). Luke 16:16 says "the law and the prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached." John belonged to the old era; Jesus inaugurates the new.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### v. 21a: Jesus Is Baptised

Jesus was not baptised because He had sins to repent of. Matthew 3:14–15 records John's reluctance and Jesus' reply: "it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness." Jesus identified completely with sinful humanity — a foreshadowing of the cross where that identification would be made complete. Luke places Jesus' baptism as the climax of John's ministry ("when all the people were baptized"), not merely as one among many.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus

---

### vv. 21b–22: The Trinity Manifested at the Baptism

Luke alone notes that Jesus was **praying** when heaven opened. Throughout his Gospel, Luke emphasises Jesus' prayer life at every crucial moment (baptism, choosing the Twelve, Transfiguration, Gethsemane, the cross). John Piper suggests Jesus was likely praying for the Holy Spirit's empowering for His public ministry (cf. Luke 11:13).

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

**The Holy Spirit descended "in bodily form like a dove."** Only Luke includes the phrase "in bodily form," which lends weight to the idea that the Spirit assumed a visible, tangible form — not that the Spirit *became* a dove, but descended *as* a dove descends. Piper observes that the dove symbolises meekness, purity, and innocence (cf. Matthew 10:16: "innocent as doves"). This directed Jesus toward a ministry of dove-like gentleness — not breaking bruised reeds or quenching smouldering wicks (Isaiah 42:1–4).

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/3.htm

**The voice from heaven:** "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased" combines two Old Testament texts:
- "You are My Son" echoes Psalm 2:7 (the royal Messianic Psalm).
- "In You I am well pleased" echoes Isaiah 42:1 (the Suffering Servant).

Together they declare Jesus as both the Davidic King and the Suffering Servant. The three Persons of the Trinity are simultaneously manifest: the Father speaks, the Spirit descends, the Son is baptised.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### v. 23a: "About Thirty Years Old"

Thirty was the age at which Levites began their full service (Numbers 4:2–3), with a probationary period from age 25 (Numbers 8:24). Priests could serve at 30, and it was generally considered the age of full manhood in Jewish culture. Jesus waited in patient humility until this age before launching His public work.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/3.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

---

### vv. 23b–38: The Genealogy of Jesus

**"(As was supposed) the son of Joseph"** — Luke's parenthetical "as was supposed" signals that Jesus was not biologically Joseph's son (given the virgin birth in Luke 1:34–35), though legally He was regarded as such.

**Differences from Matthew's genealogy:**

From David to Jesus, Matthew and Luke give almost entirely different names. Matthew traces through Solomon; Luke traces through Nathan (another son of David, 2 Samuel 5:14). Two main traditional explanations exist:

1. **Matthew gives Joseph's legal line (the royal line of succession through Solomon); Luke gives Mary's biological line (through Nathan).** On this view, Heli was Mary's father, and Joseph was his son-in-law — "son" being used loosely for "son-in-law." This is a widely held conservative Protestant view. (David Guzik / Enduring Word)
   - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/

2. **Matthew gives Joseph's legal descent; Luke gives Joseph's natural descent.** Both are Joseph's genealogies, but Matthew traces legal heirs to the throne while Luke traces actual physical descent. At some point the lines merged (e.g., through a levirate marriage or through an heir from Nathan's line becoming the legal heir when Solomon's line died out). John Piper notes this is the "more probable" view.
   - https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus

Both explanations affirm that Jesus is genuinely descended from David through both legal and biological lines, satisfying Messianic requirements. Piper quotes I. H. Marshall that "the problem caused by the existence of the two genealogies is insoluble with the evidence presently at our disposal," meaning no single solution can be proved definitively, but the two do not represent an irresolvable contradiction.

**Why Luke traces back to Adam:** Matthew stops at Abraham (writing for a Jewish audience). Luke, writing for Gentiles, traces Jesus all the way to Adam — showing Jesus belongs to **all humanity**, not only to Israel. He is the Saviour of all mankind.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-3/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus

**"Adam, the son of God"** — Luke ends by calling Adam "son of God," not in the same sense as Jesus' unique eternal Sonship (Luke 1:35), but as one directly created by God. Piper notes this sets up the parallel between Adam and Jesus as the "second Adam" (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:45–49). Where the first Adam failed, Jesus — the new Adam — would succeed, creating a new humanity marked not by ethnicity but by the Spirit.

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/3.htm

**Notes on specific names — v. 27: Zerubbabel and Shealtiel.** Zerubbabel was the leader of the first Jewish exiles returning from Babylon and oversaw the rebuilding of the Temple (Ezra 3:2). His inclusion anchors the genealogy in known post-exilic history.

**Notes on the word "son":** In the Greek of vv. 24–38, the word "son" (*huios*) is not actually repeated; the text simply uses the genitive case ("of Heli, of Matthat, of Levi…"). Jewish genealogies frequently skipped generations, so the genealogy does not provide a basis for calculating the age of the earth (contra Ussher chronology).

- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baptism-and-the-genealogy-of-jesus

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

| Verse | Issue | Pentecostal / Charismatic | Reformed / Baptist | Older / Classic |
|-------|-------|--------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **v. 16** | "Baptize with Holy Spirit and fire" | Spirit baptism = post-conversion empowerment, evidenced by tongues (AG). Fire = purifying presence | Spirit baptism = incorporation into Christ's body at conversion. Fire = judgment on the unrepentant (Ligonier, Piper) | Fire = purification, not judgment; the "fire" explains the "Spirit" (Pulpit Commentary) |
| **vv. 23–38** | Genealogy | Generally hold Mary's line (Guzik) or Joseph's natural line (Piper) | Same options; no distinct tradition | Ellicott surveys all solutions; notes that "volumes have been written" |
